q-126844.source_problem: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ about the point $x=2.$
q-126844.source_quote:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ and $a=2.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ f(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =-\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+(\frac{1}{2})(x-2)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{4})(x-2)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\frac{1}{2}(x-2)-\frac{1}{8}(x-2)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ about the point $x=2.$
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ and $a=2.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ f(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =-\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+(\frac{1}{2})(x-2)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{4})(x-2)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\frac{1}{2}(x-2)-\frac{1}{8}(x-2)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-126874.source_problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ about $x=\pi $ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ Give your answer to $5$ decimal places.
q-126874.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =(0)+(-1)(x-\pi )+\frac{(0)}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}+\frac{(1)}{3!}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯ \\  & =-(x-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=3$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡3 & ≈-(3-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(3-\pi )^{3} \\  & =0.141\,12,\end{aligned}
$$

to five decimal places.

fields.binding: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ about $x=\pi $ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ Give your answer to $5$ decimal places.
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =(0)+(-1)(x-\pi )+\frac{(0)}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}+\frac{(1)}{3!}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯ \\  & =-(x-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=3$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡3 & ≈-(3-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(3-\pi )^{3} \\  & =0.141\,12,\end{aligned}
$$

to five decimal places.

q-126877.source_problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
q-126877.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =1+(2)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{(4)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}) & ≈1+2(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =1+2(-\frac{\pi }{20})+2{(-\frac{\pi }{20})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{10}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{200} \\  & =0.735\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

fields.binding: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =1+(2)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{(4)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}) & ≈1+2(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})+2{(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =1+2(-\frac{\pi }{20})+2{(-\frac{\pi }{20})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{10}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{200} \\  & =0.735\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

q-126995.source_problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(2,3,6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-3,-2,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
q-126995.source_quote:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

fields.binding: Direction normsqrt14, distance|t|sqrt14 implies t+-1; pointsP+-v=(-1,1,7),(5,5,5).
fields.source_quote:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

q-126998.source_problem:
Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4t \\ y=-2t \\ z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

What would be the vector equation of the line?
q-126998.source_quote:
These parametric equations are equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4t \\ -2t \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ -2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

fields.binding:
Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4t \\ y=-2t \\ z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

What would be the vector equation of the line?
fields.source_quote:
These parametric equations are equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4t \\ -2t \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ -2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

$$

fields.binding:
Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=5-9t \\ y=-2+7t \\ z=-8t\end{aligned}
$$

What would be the vector equation of the line?
fields.source_quote:
These parametric equations are equivalent to 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5-9t \\ -2+7t \\ -8t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-9t \\ 7t \\ -8t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 7 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 7 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

$$

q-127373.source_problem: A deck contains $10$ cards labeled with the numbers $4$, $7$, $10,…,31.$ If one card is randomly drawn from the deck, what is its expected value?
q-127373.source_quote:
The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Let $X$ be the number on a randomly drawn card. Then the support is $S={4,7,10,…,31},$ and the corresponding probabilities are all $\frac{1}{10}:$

$$
f(4)=f(7)=f(10)=…=f(31)=\frac{1}{10}
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =4\cdot f(4)+7\cdot f(7)+10\cdot f(10)+…+31\cdot f(10) \\  & =\frac{4}{10}+\frac{7}{10}+\frac{10}{10}+…+\frac{31}{10} \\  & =\frac{4+7+10+13+16+19+22+25+28+31}{10} \\  & =\frac{175}{10} \\  & =17.5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127770.source_problem:
Consider a game of chance with $4$ prizes ($$1$, $$2$, $$3$, and $$4$) where each outcome has a specific probability of happening, shown in the table below. 

| $\text{Number}$ | $\text{Probability}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $$1$ | $40%$ |
| $$2$ | $30%$ |
| $$3$ | $20%$ |
| $$4$ | $10%$ |

What is the expected profit per game?
q-127770.source_quote:
Let $p$ represent the profit on a single game. Using the given probabilities, let's summarize this in a table.  If $p$ is the profit (in dollars) on a single game, and $f(p)$ is the probability mass function for $p,$ then we have the following:

| $f(p)$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ | $\frac{3}{10}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $p$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Therefore, the expected value of $p$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[p] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =1(\frac{2}{5})+2(\frac{3}{10})+3(\frac{1}{5})+4(\frac{1}{10}) \\  & =\frac{4}{10}+\frac{6}{10}+\frac{6}{10}+\frac{4}{10} \\  & =\frac{20}{10} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the expected profit is $$2.$

q-127826.source_problem:
Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 9\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 15 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
q-127826.source_quote:
- The matrix $A$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix. So, it is not invertible.

- For the matrix $B$, we have

$$
det(B)=-3\cdot 5-1\cdot 15=-30.
$$

Because $det(B)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $B$ is invertible.

- For the matrix $C$, we have

$$
det(C)=7\cdot 2-3\cdot 4=2.
$$

Because $det(C)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $C$ is invertible.

Therefore, only $A$ does not have an inverse.

q-128139.source_problem:
Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

*If a $2\times 2$-matrix $A$ is invertible, then $\text{__________}$ . *

- $det(A)\ne 0$
- $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution
- $Ax=0$ has infinitely many solutions
q-128139.source_quote:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

Now, since the first part of the invertible matrix theorem is true ($A$ is invertible), all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem, only options I and III give us true statements:

- *If $A$ is invertible, then $det(A)\ne 0.$* $\,✓$

- *If $A$ is invertible, then $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$* $\,✓$

q-128461.source_problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨{k}^{2},7,4⟩,$ $b=⟨6,7,4⟩,$ and $c=⟨3,0,2⟩$ are coplanar.
q-128461.source_quote:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & 7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|-7\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}(7\cdot 2-0\cdot 4)-7(6\cdot 2-3\cdot 4)+4(6\cdot 0-3\cdot 7) \\  & =14{k}^{2}+0-84 \\  & =14{k}^{2}-84 \\  & =14({k}^{2}-6).\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 14({k}^{2}-6) & =0 \\ {k}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ {k}^{2} & =6 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\sqrt{6}$ or $k=\sqrt{6}.$

$$

$$

Since $det(F)=7$, the matrix is **not** singular. 

Therefore, only statement II is true.

$[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & m \\ m & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
is $-29$, find all the possible values of $m.$
q-128506.source_quote:
Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & m \\ m & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-6|\begin{aligned}m & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|+m|\begin{aligned}m & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-0)-6(m-0)+m(m-6) \\  & =3-6m+{m}^{2}-6m \\  & ={m}^{2}-12m+3\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $-29,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12m+3 & =-29 \\ {m}^{2}-12m+32 & =0 \\ m & =\frac{-(-12)\pm \sqrt{{12}^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 32}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{12\pm \sqrt{16}}{2} \\  & =\frac{12\pm 4}{2} \\  & =6\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $m=4$ and $m=8.$

q-128519.source_problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x,$ find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$
q-128519.source_quote:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =-\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{y})j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x})j=0\,i+0\,j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1=0 \\ \frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{{(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ 9\cdot {(-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})}^{2}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81+3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}} & =0 \\ 81+3{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-27 \\ x & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-3,$ we get $y=-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{3}=-3.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point: $(-3,-3).$

q-129129.source_problem:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 & 6 \\ 4 & 1 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$
q-129129.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$ and  $y$,  the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}0x+8y=6 \\ 4x+y=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

By simplifying, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}8y=6 \\ 4x+y=-9.\end{aligned}

fields.binding:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 & 6 \\ 4 & 1 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$ and  $y$,  the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}0x+8y=6 \\ 4x+y=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

By simplifying, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}8y=6 \\ 4x+y=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

q-129133.source_problem:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 4 & -\frac{7}{4} \\ 0 & 5 & \frac{2}{3} & 8 \\ \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{3} & 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$
q-129133.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$, $y$, and $z,$ then, the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}0x-8y+4z=-\frac{7}{4} \\ 0x+5y+\frac{2}{3}z=8 \\ \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{3}y+4z=6.\end{aligned}
$$

By simplifying, we obtain 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-8y+4z=-\frac{7}{4} \\ 5y+\frac{2}{3}z=8 \\ \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{3}y+4z=6.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 4 & -\frac{7}{4} \\ 0 & 5 & \frac{2}{3} & 8 \\ \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{3} & 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$, $y$, and $z,$ then, the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}0x-8y+4z=-\frac{7}{4} \\ 0x+5y+\frac{2}{3}z=8 \\ \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{3}y+4z=6.\end{aligned}
$$

By simplifying, we obtain 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-8y+4z=-\frac{7}{4} \\ 5y+\frac{2}{3}z=8 \\ \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{3}y+4z=6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{3z}{x+6y} & =c \\ 3z & =c(x+6y) \\ 3z & =cx+6cy \\ z & =\frac{c}{3}x+2cy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of planes:

$$
z=\frac{c}{3}x+2cy,\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

q-129198.source_quote:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y+z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & ={e}^{c}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x-2y+z={r}^{2},\,r\in (-\infty ,\infty )

fields.binding: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y+z)?$
fields.source_quote:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y+z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & ={e}^{c}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the exponent ${e}^{c}$ is positive for all $-\infty <c<\infty .$ If we let ${e}^{c}={r}^{2},$ we get a family of planes:

$$
x-2y+z={r}^{2},\,r\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

q-129213.source_problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -9\end{aligned}].
$$
q-129213.source_quote:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are in row echelon form.

fields.binding: A repeats pivotcol5 lasttwo rows, fails; Bpivot1,3 thenzero; Cpivot2,3,4 thenzero; BandC.
fields.source_quote:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${a}_{45}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ and $C$ are in row echelon form.

q-129224.source_problem:
The intersection of the planes $2x-y-3z-8=0$ and $x+2y-3z-4=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
q-129224.source_quote:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
2x-y-3(0)-8=0\,⟹\,y=2x-8,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $y=2x-8$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(2x-8)-0-4 & =0 \\ x+4x-16-4 & =0 \\ 5x & =20 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=2(4)-8=0$ and $a=⟨4,0,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $2x-y-3z-8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,-1,-3⟩.$

- For the plane $x+2y-3z-4=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨2,-1,-3⟩\times ⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =9i+3j+5k \\  & =⟨9,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨4,0,0⟩+t⟨9,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=4+0=4,$ and $b=⟨9,3,5⟩.$

fields.binding:
The intersection of the planes $2x-y-3z-8=0$ and $x+2y-3z-4=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
fields.source_quote:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
2x-y-3(0)-8=0\,⟹\,y=2x-8,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $y=2x-8$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(2x-8)-0-4 & =0 \\ x+4x-16-4 & =0 \\ 5x & =20 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=2(4)-8=0$ and $a=⟨4,0,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $2x-y-3z-8=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,-1,-3⟩.$

- For the plane $x+2y-3z-4=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨2,-1,-3⟩\times ⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =9i+3j+5k \\  & =⟨9,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨4,0,0⟩+t⟨9,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=4+0=4,$ and $b=⟨9,3,5⟩.$

q-129231.source_problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$
q-129231.source_quote:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since ${b}_{33}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are **not** in row echelon form.

q-130005.source_problem:
Consider the differential equation $x{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}+4{x}^{3}y=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ is a solution to the equation
- ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation
- The general solution of the equation is $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}$
q-130005.source_quote:
Let's check each statement:

- To determine whether ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute ${y}_{1}$ and its derivatives into the equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
x(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+4{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=(4{x}^{3}-4x)\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{1}$ is not a solution to the equation, and therefore statement II is false.

- Similarly, we compute the derivatives of ${y}_{2}$ and substitute to the equation. Computing the derivatives yields

First, we find the first and second derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation. We get

$$
x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2})-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}=(2x-2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2}+(4{x}^{3}-4{x}^{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}=0.\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{2}$ is a solution to the equation, and therefore statement II is true.

- So, ${y}_{2}$ is a solution while ${y}_{1}$ is not a solution of the equation, hence $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}$  is not the general solution.

Therefore, statement III is false.

q-130217.source_problem: At which points on the curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2y-2x$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $-i+j?$
q-130217.source_quote:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $-i+j,$ we must have $t\cdot (-i+j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ ((2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ -(2y-2)-(2x+2) & =0 \\ -2y-2x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+(-x)^{2} & =2(-x)-2x \\ 2{x}^{2} & =-4x \\ 2{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ 2x(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- For $x=-2,$ we get $y=2,$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$

- For $x=0,$ we get $y=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

fields.source_quote:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $-i+j,$ we must have $t\cdot (-i+j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ ((2y-2)\,i-(2x+2)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) & =0 \\ -(2y-2)-(2x+2) & =0 \\ -2y-2x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y-2x \\ {x}^{2}+(-x)^{2} & =2(-x)-2x \\ 2{x}^{2} & =-4x \\ 2{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ 2x(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- For $x=-2,$ we get $y=2,$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$

- For $x=0,$ we get $y=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

q-130256.source_problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
- ${D}_{3}(y)={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
q-130256.source_quote:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is **not** linear. To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2}) & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =2a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}-bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+2bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-130448.source_problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 3 \\ -5 & 8 & -7 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 11 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

By applying elementary row operations of the form ${R}_{i}:={R}_{i}+k{R}_{1},$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the elementary row operations?
q-130448.source_quote:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make the entries below ${a}_{12}=-2$ equal to $0.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary row operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 3 \\ -5 & 8 & -7 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 11 & 0 & 5 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 11 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elementary row operations are

What is the system of equations represented by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?
$$
q-130528.source_quote:
The  $2\times 2$ matrix represents the coefficients of $x$ and $y,$ while the $2\times 1$ column vector on the right-hand side represents the constants of the equations. So, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}0x+5y=9 \\ x+0y=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying both equations in the system, we get

$$

fields.binding:
What is the system of equations represented by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?
$$
fields.source_quote:
The  $2\times 2$ matrix represents the coefficients of $x$ and $y,$ while the $2\times 1$ column vector on the right-hand side represents the constants of the equations. So, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}0x+5y=9 \\ x+0y=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying both equations in the system, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}5y=9 \\ x=-1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & -2 & 8 \\ -6 & 9 & -3 & 7 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 & -8 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -5 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & -4 \\ -1 & 10 & 3 & 15\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $B$ above. By applying three matrix elementary column operations 

- ${C}_{1}:=…$
- ${C}_{2}:={C}_{2}+2{C}_{3}$
- ${C}_{4}:=…$

each of the form ${C}_{i}:={C}_{i}+k{C}_{3},$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the missing elementary column operations?
q-130624.source_quote:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make entries to the left and to the right of ${a}_{13}=-2$ equal to $0.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary column operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & -2 & 8 \\ -6 & 9 & -3 & 7 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 & -8 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:={C}_{1}-2{C}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 8 \\ 0 & 9 & -3 & 7 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -8 \\ -1 & 4 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{2}:={C}_{2}+2{C}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & -8 \\ -1 & 10 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{4}:={C}_{4}+4{C}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -5 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & -4 \\ -1 & 10 & 3 & 15\end{aligned}] \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding elementary column operations are

$\,$ ${C}_{1}:={C}_{1}-2{C}_{3}\,$ and $\,{C}_{4}:={C}_{4}+4{C}_{3}.$

q-130772.source_problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,S=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
q-130772.source_quote:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrices $P$ and $Q$ are not elementary matrices because they can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $S$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =S\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $S$ is an elementary matrix.

q-130927.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+2y-z=4 \\  & -3x-6y+4z=-8 \\  & 3x+7y-z=10.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-130927.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z=4 \\ y+2z=-2 \\ z=4,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2(4)=-2\,⟹\,y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-10$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(-10)-(4)=4\,⟹\,x=28.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=28$, $y=-10$, and $z=4.$

The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z=4 \\ y+2z=-2 \\ z=4,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2(4)=-2\,⟹\,y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-10$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(-10)-(4)=4\,⟹\,x=28.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=28$, $y=-10$, and $z=4.$

If a second-order differential equation for the function $y(x)$ is given with two conditions specified at the *same* location in the domain of $y,$ then this is an **initial value problem**.

- The second system is not an initial value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=0$ and $x=1$). This is a **boundary value problem.**

- The third system is an initial value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the same location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$).

q-131030.source_problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\sqrt{x}$ are solutions to the equation $2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+3x{y}^{′}-y=0$ for $x>0,$ what function must also be a solution to the given differential equation?
q-131030.source_quote:
According to the superposition principle, if the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are solutions to a homogeneous, linear differential equation, and ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are constants, then $y(x)={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x)$ is also a solution to the equation.

We're given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore, the following function is also a solution:

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\frac{1}{x}+{c}_{2}\sqrt{x}
$$

If we let ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get:

$$
y(x)=\frac{2}{x}+\sqrt{x}=\frac{2+x\sqrt{x}}{x}
$$

fields.binding: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}$ are solutions to the equation ${y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-2y=0,$ what function must also be a solution to the given differential equation?
fields.source_quote:
According to the superposition principle, if the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are solutions to a homogeneous, linear differential equation, and ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are constants, then $y(x)={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x)$ is also a solution to the equation.

We're given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}.$ Therefore, the following function is also a solution:

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{e}^{x}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2x}
$$

If we let ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}$ and ${c}_{2}=-\frac{1}{3},$ we get:

$$
y(x)=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{3}=\frac{2{e}^{x}-{e}^{-2x}}{3}
$$

q-131188.source_problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-72x.$
q-131188.source_quote:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-72x) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-6x-72.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-6x-72 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x-12 & =0 \\ (x-4)(x+3) & =0 \\ x & =-3,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-3$ and $x=4.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-3$ and $x=4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(8{x}^{3}-8x){e}^{4{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{3}-8x & =0 \\ 8x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 8x(x+1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,-1,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

q-131302.source_problem:
What are the pivot columns of the matrix $P,$ given by

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]?
$$
q-131302.source_quote:
First, we need to convert $P$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{4} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $P$ has $3$ pivots. In particular, the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns.

q-131485.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-131485.source_quote:
Notice that the matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form. The system corresponding to $M$ is 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+0y+7z=-3 \\ 0x+y-2z=2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+7z=-3 \\ y-2z=2\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ To do this, we apply the back substitution. 

From the second equation, we get

$$
y-2z=2\,⇒\,y=2z+2
$$

and from the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+7z=-3\,⇒\,x=-7z-3.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-7z-3 \\ y=2z+2 \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7z-3 \\ 2z+2 \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
fields.source_quote:
Notice that the matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form. The system corresponding to $M$ is 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+0y+7z=-3 \\ 0x+y-2z=2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+7z=-3 \\ y-2z=2\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ To do this, we apply the back substitution. 

From the second equation, we get

$$
y-2z=2\,⇒\,y=2z+2
$$

and from the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+7z=-3\,⇒\,x=-7z-3.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-7z-3 \\ y=2z+2 \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

q-131499.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -8 & 6 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-131499.source_quote:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x-8y+6z=-4 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
2x-8y+6z=-4
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=4y-3z-2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -8 & 6 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
fields.source_quote:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x-8y+6z=-4 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
2x-8y+6z=-4
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=4y-3z-2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-131502.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-131502.source_quote:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-3y+2z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-3y+2z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=3y-2z-1.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3y-2z-1 \\ y=y \\ z=z\end{aligned}
$$

where $y,z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3y-2z-1 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
fields.source_quote:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -6 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-3y+2z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-3y+2z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=3y-2z-1.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3y-2z-1 \\ y=y \\ z=z\end{aligned}
$$

where $y,z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3y-2z-1 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-131650.source_problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4x-8y+12z=-8 \\ x-2y+3z=-2 \\ -2x+4y-6z=4\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-131650.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4x-8y+12z=-8 \\ x-2y+3z=-2 \\ -2x+4y-6z=4\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-131712.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 2x+8y=-6 \\  & -4x-16y=12 \\  & 6x+24y=-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-131712.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -6 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -6 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+4y=-3\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$  in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-4y-3 \\ y=y,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4y-3 \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 2x+8y=-6 \\  & -4x-16y=12 \\  & 6x+24y=-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -6 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 & -6 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ -4 & -16 & 12 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 24 & -18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now  

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+4y=-3\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$  in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-4y-3 \\ y=y,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4y-3 \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-131720.source_problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 2x-6y-2z=4 \\  & 3x-9y-3z=6\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- The system is consistent independent
- The system has no solution
- The system is consistent dependent
q-131720.source_quote:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x,$ and we have two free variables, $y$ and $z.$ That means we can find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*. 

As a result, only statement III is true.

q-131721.source_problem:
Consider the following system of equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+2y=-1 \\  & 3x+7y=1 \\  & -2x-4y=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- The system is consistent independent
- The system has no solution
- The system is consistent dependent
q-131721.source_quote:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 7 & 1 \\ -2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 7 & 1 \\ -2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the third equation $0x+0y=0$, we can remove this equation from the system. So, the corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y=-1 \\ y=4.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation we have $y=4$ and substituting this into the first equation yields $x=-9.$ So,  we conclude that the system is consistent independent. 

As a result, only statement I is true.

Consider the following system of equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 3x-3y=6 \\  & -2x+y=-3 \\  & 4x-4y=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- The system is consistent dependent
- The system is consistent independent
- The system has no solution
q-131722.source_quote:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 6 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 6 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the third equation $0x+0y=0$, we can remove this equation from the system. So, the corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y=2 \\ y=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation we have $y=-1$ and substituting this into the first equation yields $x=1.$ So,  we conclude that the system is consistent independent. 

As a result, only statement II is true.

q-132204.source_problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,0)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$
q-132204.source_quote:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,0⟩,$ since the point $P(0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,0⟩+1\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}

fields.source_quote:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,0⟩,$ since the point $P(0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,0⟩+1\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-132666.source_problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}$ is strictly decreasing.
q-132666.source_quote:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6)<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to

$$
4x-6<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-6 & <0 \\ 4x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,\frac{3}{2}).$

q-132667.source_quote:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 4x \\  & =\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1}<0.
$$

The function $2{x}^{2}+1$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
4x<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

fields.binding: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)$ is strictly decreasing.
fields.source_quote:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 4x \\  & =\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1}<0.
$$

The function $2{x}^{2}+1$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
4x<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

q-132852.source_problem:
The lifetime of a lithium-ion battery produced by a particular company is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ years and a standard deviation of $0.5$ years.
Additionally, $3%$ of batteries last less than $1.75$ years. Find the mean $\mu $, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |
q-132852.source_quote:
Let $X$ represent the lifetime of a randomly selected battery. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.5}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(X<1.75)=0.03.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.75) & =0.03 \\ P(Z\le \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ Φ(\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.03).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.03)=-1.8808.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & =-1.8808 \\ 1.75-\mu  & =-0.9404 \\ \mu  & ≈2.69.\end{aligned}
$$

q-132856.source_problem:
A cinema admission fee is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ dollars and a standard deviation of $$0.7.$ In addition, in $94%$ of cases the admission fee is between $$0.75\mu $ and $$1.25\mu .$ Find the average cinema admission fee, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |
q-132856.source_quote:
Let $X$ represent an admission fee. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.7}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.75\mu <X<1.25\mu )=0.94.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.75\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.94 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.94 \\ P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.47 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.5+0.47 \\ P(X<1.25\mu ) & =0.97\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.25\mu ) & =0.97 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7}) & =0.97 \\ Φ(\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7}) & =0.97 \\ \frac{0.25\mu }{0.7} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.97)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.97)≈1.8808.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7} & =1.8808 \\ 0.25\mu  & =1.31656 \\ \mu  & =\frac{1.31656}{0.25} \\  & ≈5.27.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=axy-5{y}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}-bxy.
$$
q-133221.source_quote:

$$

$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}ax-10y=2x-by.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13944892/assets/ce3aec85d418c8f51988f819c04403f3f3ea2e0c0e35165ed729fc1e78d0f12f.png)

The scatter plot shows the value of an artwork $y,$ in thousands of dollars, and the number of decades $x$ since it was first created. The equation of the trend line is $y=3x+5.$ 

Assuming this trend continues, estimate the time it takes for the artwork to be worth $$32\,000.$
q-133929.source_quote:
To predict the time that must pass before the artwork is worth $$32\,000,$ we need to substitute $y=32$ into the equation of the trend line and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x+5 \\ 32 & =3x+5 \\ 3x & =27 \\ x & =9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, according to this model, it takes approximately $9$ decades for the artwork to have a value of $$32\,000.$ 

Note: The point where $y=32$ is not shown on our trend line. Therefore, our result *may* be unreliable.

q-135228.source_problem:
A marble is projected vertically downward from a height of $245\,\text{m}$ with an initial velocity of $24.5\,\text{m/s}.$ How long will it take for the marble to hit the ground? 

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*
q-135228.source_quote:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the marble is $u=24.5\,\text{m/s}.$

- The marble covers the distance of $s=245\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ 245 & =(24.5)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 245 & =24.5t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50(4.9) & =5(4.9)t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50\cancel{(4.9)} & =5\cancel{(4.9)}t+\cancel{(4.9)}{t}^{2} \\ 50 & =5t+{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+5t-50 & =0 \\ (t+10)(t-5) & =0 \\ t & =-10,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the marble hits the ground after $t=5$ seconds.

fields.binding:
A marble is projected vertically downward from a height of $245\,\text{m}$ with an initial velocity of $24.5\,\text{m/s}.$ How long will it take for the marble to hit the ground? 

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*
fields.source_quote:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the marble is $u=24.5\,\text{m/s}.$

- The marble covers the distance of $s=245\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ 245 & =(24.5)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 245 & =24.5t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50(4.9) & =5(4.9)t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50\cancel{(4.9)} & =5\cancel{(4.9)}t+\cancel{(4.9)}{t}^{2} \\ 50 & =5t+{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+5t-50 & =0 \\ (t+10)(t-5) & =0 \\ t & =-10,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the marble hits the ground after $t=5$ seconds.
