q-168921.source_problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the finite region bounded between the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=1?$

- It is a type I region
- It is a type II region
- It's neither a type I nor a type II region
q-168921.source_quote:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038811/assets/bc6b71d1fe69abd34dbd939dc62ede5201b75713e25456cf084e889bc44f449e.png)

We have the following:

- The vertical line $x=0.4$ intersects the region in two separate intervals, as shown below. So, this can't be a type I region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038811/assets/4a1fd7069abaa3b3fa4d9c286773d226798bf3ad565e85663cab44557fd635c1.png)

- The horizontal line $y=-1$ intersects the region in two separate intervals, as shown below. So, this can't be a type II region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038811/assets/260e8e959ca95a029a98bd4102106a66df418ea73c0640398c8fdebfdbf812f6.png)

Therefore, only statement III is true.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931416/assets/71d9df0708a77639f3f7b2640ea2a03cebbfd72e6cfb3369c07d83a89eba6508.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
q-170347.source_quote:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1.$ Therefore, $c=-1.$

fields.source_quote:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1.$ Therefore, $c=-1.$

q-170558.source_problem: Calculate the $x$-coordinates of the points where the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1$ intersects the line $y=8x.$
q-170558.source_quote:
To find the points where the hyperbola intersects the line $y=8x,$ we first replace $y$ with $8x$ in the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{(8x)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-4{x}^{2} & =1 \\ -3{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot take the square root of a negative number. Therefore, the equation has no real solutions. So, the hyperbola does not intersect the line $y=8x.$

q-171016.source_problem:
$\,$ $3\,|\,18$ or $11$ is not prime.

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
q-171016.source_quote:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(3\,|\,18\text{ or }11\text{ is not prime}) & ≡¬((3\,|\,18)∨(11\text{ is not prime})) \\  & ≡¬(3\,|\,18)∧¬(11\text{ is not prime}) \\  & ≡(3\,\text{⧸}|\,18)∧(11\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡3\,\text{⧸}|\,18\text{ and }11\text{ is prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Negate the disjunction using De Morgan: negate divisibility and negate not-prime, giving 3 does not divide 18 AND 11 is prime.
fields.source_quote:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(3\,|\,18\text{ or }11\text{ is not prime}) & ≡¬((3\,|\,18)∨(11\text{ is not prime})) \\  & ≡¬(3\,|\,18)∧¬(11\text{ is not prime}) \\  & ≡(3\,\text{⧸}|\,18)∧(11\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡3\,\text{⧸}|\,18\text{ and }11\text{ is prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-17392.source_problem: Given that $y=2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1.$
q-17392.source_quote:
To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x) \\  & =2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =2e\cdot {1}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =2e-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-17544.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{x}
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
q-17544.source_quote:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{z}^{-1}+2{x}^{2}{z}^{-2}}{x} \\ -\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{xz}+\frac{2x}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-2x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-2{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x} \\ y & =\frac{3x}{C-2{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-176051.source_problem:
Given the statement

$$
P:3\text{ is smaller than }5
$$

 
which of the following represents $¬P?$
q-176051.source_quote:
The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is not true that }3\text{ is smaller than }5.
$$

 

In other words, $3$ is *not* smaller than $5.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:3\text{ is }\text{not}\text{ smaller than }5.
$$

 

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

q-18244.source_problem:
Given that the minor of ${a}_{22}$ is $-70$, find all the possible values of $k$ in the matrix

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2k & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 5 & -7 \\ 11 & 9 & k+3\end{aligned}].
$$
q-18244.source_quote:
First, we remove the second row and second column:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2k & ∗ & 6 \\ ∗ & 5 & ∗ \\ 11 & ∗ & k+3\end{aligned}]
$$

The minor of ${a}_{22}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}2k & 6 \\ 11 & k+3\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}2k & 6 \\ 11 & k+3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2k\cdot (k+3)-11\cdot 6 \\  & =2{k}^{2}+6k-66.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of ${a}_{22}$ is $-70$, so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{k}^{2}+6k-66 & =-70 \\ 2{k}^{2}+6k+4 & =0 \\ {k}^{2}+3k+2 & =0 \\ (k+1)(k+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}2k & 6 \\ 11 & k+3\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}2k & 6 \\ 11 & k+3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2k\cdot (k+3)-11\cdot 6 \\  & =2{k}^{2}+6k-66.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of ${a}_{22}$ is $-70$, so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{k}^{2}+6k-66 & =-70 \\ 2{k}^{2}+6k+4 & =0 \\ {k}^{2}+3k+2 & =0 \\ (k+1)(k+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $k=-1$ and $k=-2.$

q-182445.source_problem:
$\,$ $|{1,x}|\ne 0$ and $x$ is rational

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
q-182445.source_quote:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(|{1,x}|\ne 0\text{ and }x\text{ is rational}) & ≡¬((|{1,x}|\ne 0)∧(x\text{ is rational})) \\  & ≡¬(|{1,x}|\ne 0)∨¬(x\text{ is rational}) \\  & ≡(|{1,x}|=0)∨(x\text{ is not rational}) \\  & ≡|{1,x}|=0\text{ or }x\text{ is not rational}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-182450.source_problem:
$\,$ $2$ is not prime or $2\notin Q.$

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
q-182450.source_quote:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(2\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }2\notin Q) & ≡¬((2\text{ is not prime})∨(2\notin Q)) \\  & ≡¬(2\text{ is not prime})∧¬(2\notin Q) \\  & ≡(2\text{ is prime})∧(2\in Q) \\  & ≡2\text{ is prime}\text{ and }2\in Q.\end{aligned}
$$

q-18246.source_problem:
Given that the minor of ${p}_{23}$ is ${t}^{2}+12$, find all the possible values of $t$ in the matrix

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}t & -8 & 3 \\ -7 & 4 & 4 \\ -1 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
q-18246.source_quote:
First, we remove the second row and third column:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}t & -8 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗ & 4 \\ -1 & 9 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

The minor of ${p}_{23}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot 9-(-8)\cdot (-1) \\  & =9t-8.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of ${p}_{23}$ is ${t}^{2}+12$, so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}9t-8 & ={t}^{2}+12 \\ {t}^{2}-9t+20 & =0 \\ (t-5)(t-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=4$ and $t=5.$

fields.source_quote:
First, we remove the second row and third column:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}t & -8 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗ & 4 \\ -1 & 9 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

The minor of ${p}_{23}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}[\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}] & =|\begin{aligned}t & -8 \\ -1 & 9\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot 9-(-8)\cdot (-1) \\  & =9t-8.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the minor of ${p}_{23}$ is ${t}^{2}+12$, so we must have:

$$
\begin{aligned}9t-8 & ={t}^{2}+12 \\ {t}^{2}-9t+20 & =0 \\ (t-5)(t-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=4$ and $t=5.$

q-182507.source_problem:
$\,$ If you exercise regularly, then you'll improve your health.

Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?
q-182507.source_quote:
Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A:$ You exercise regularly.

- $B:$ You will improve your health.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A⇒B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬A∨B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $¬A:$ You do not exercise regularly.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ You do not exercise regularly, or you will improve your health.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\,$ Either you do not exercise regularly, or you'll improve your health.

**Note**: 

Using the word "Either" helps clarify that the sentence structure presents two alternatives and is particularly useful when employing the disjunctive form $(¬P∨Q)$ in conversational or formal English. So, the phrase effectively conveys that one of the two stated conditions will hold true.

q-183349.source_problem:
$\,$ If $x\in N,$ then  $x$ is positive.

Which of the following is logically equivalent to the conditional predicate above?
q-183349.source_quote:
Let's denote by $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x\in N.$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is positive.

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x\notin N.$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ $x\notin N,$ or $x$ is positive.

q-183452.source_problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ For all $t\in Q,$ $t<1.$
q-183452.source_quote:
If we denote

$$
P(t):t<1,
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∀t\in Q,\,P(t).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$

q-183463.source_problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ All prime numbers are not divisible by $5.$
q-183463.source_quote:
Let $P$ be the set of prime numbers. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ For all $x\in P,$ $x$ is not divisible by $5.$

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\,$ $∀x\in P,\,x\text{ is not divisible by }5.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀x\in P,\,x\text{ is not divisible by }5.) & ≡∃x\in P,\,¬(x\text{ is not divisible by }5.) \\  & ≡∃x\in P,\,x\text{ is divisible by }5.\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\,$ There exists $x\in P$ such that $x$ is divisible by $5.$

or simply

$\,$ Some prime numbers are divisible by $5.$

fields.binding: Original radio field 1 (selection): Existential negation requires all natural n and nonmembership of n/10.
fields.source_quote:
If we denote

$$
P(n):\frac{n}{10}\in N,
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∃n\in N,\,P(n).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
¬(∃n\in N,\,P(n))≡∀n\in N,\,¬P(n).
$$

Finally, $∀n\in N,\,¬P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $n\in N,$ $\frac{n}{10}\notin N.$

q-183515.source_problem:
$\,$ $S(x):$ ${x}^{2}=3$

Given the predicate above, which of the following expresses the statement $∃x\in Q,\,S(x)?$
q-183515.source_quote:
The existential quantifier "$∃$" means "there exists." So, the statement 
$∃x\in Q,\,S(x)$ 
reads as follows:

$\,$ **There exists** $x\in Q$ **such that** ${x}^{2}=3.$

**Note:** This statement is false.

$\,$ $∀\,ϵ\in {R}^{+},\,∃\,x\in Q,\,-ϵ<x<ϵ.$

Which of the following expresses the statement given above?

$\,$ **For all** $ϵ\in {R}^{+},$ **there exists** $x\in Q$ **such that** $-ϵ<x<ϵ.$ 

This can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ Given any real number $ϵ>0$ there exists a rational number $x$ such that $-ϵ<x<ϵ.$

q-18688.source_problem:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5\end{aligned}
$$
q-18688.source_quote:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 &  \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 15a+5b=25\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=2a-1
$$

Now, to find the value of $a,$ we can substitute $b=2a-1$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}15a+5(2a-1) & =25 \\ 15a+10a-5 & =25 \\ 25a & =30 \\ a & =\frac{30}{25} \\ a & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $a=1.2$ into the  first equation to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =2(1.2)-1 \\  & =2.4-1 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $a=1.2$ and $b=1.4.$

fields.binding:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5\end{aligned}
$$
fields.source_quote:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 &  \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 15a+5b=25\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=2a-1
$$

Now, to find the value of $a,$ we can substitute $b=2a-1$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}15a+5(2a-1) & =25 \\ 15a+10a-5 & =25 \\ 25a & =30 \\ a & =\frac{30}{25} \\ a & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $a=1.2$ into the  first equation to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =2(1.2)-1 \\  & =2.4-1 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $a=1.2$ and $b=1.4.$

q-19493.source_problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{1/3}$ about $x=8$ to approximate the value of ${7}^{1/3}.$
q-19493.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=8.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/3} \\ f(8) & ={8}^{1/3}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{3}(8)^{-2/3}=\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1/3} & =2+\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}(x-8)+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-8}{12}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=7$ into the above to approximate ${7}^{1/3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{1/3} & ≈2+\frac{7-8}{12} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{23}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{1/3}$ about $x=8$ to approximate the value of ${7}^{1/3}.$
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=8.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/3} \\ f(8) & ={8}^{1/3}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{3}(8)^{-2/3}=\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1/3} & =2+\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}(x-8)+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-8}{12}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=7$ into the above to approximate ${7}^{1/3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{1/3} & ≈2+\frac{7-8}{12} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{23}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20362.source_problem:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
q-20362.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$, $y$, and $z,$ then, the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y+2z=1 \\ 3x+2y+3z=2 \\ 4x+3y+4z=3.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$, $y$, and $z,$ then, the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y+2z=1 \\ 3x+2y+3z=2 \\ 4x+3y+4z=3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20851.source_problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2\sqrt{t},\,y=12t+1,\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
q-20851.source_quote:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=12.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{12}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}}=12\sqrt{t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =12\sqrt{1} \\  & =12\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20966.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-20966.source_quote:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y+4z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-y+4z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=-1+y-4z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1+y-4z \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1+y-4z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
fields.source_quote:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y+4z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-y+4z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=-1+y-4z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1+y-4z \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1+y-4z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-20990.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14077511/assets/5855e92b04ffbf8447d32c7edb190cd16046a13e8808e6ffaade1f59e414c869.png)

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=2t{e}^{t},\,y={t}^{2}+2t,\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
q-20990.source_quote:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{t}(t+1),\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t+2.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t+2}{2{e}^{t}(t+1)}=\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-21081.source_problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+7,\,y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+10,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.
q-21081.source_quote:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
4\operatorname{cos}⁡t=0\,⟹\,t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-4\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =4\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

fields.source_quote:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
4\operatorname{cos}⁡t=0\,⟹\,t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-4\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =4\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the tangent to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $t=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062586/assets/4aa2bca8faab077c47fb968882579233babe7d323ba3120088e8ea5599fbd570.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y=t$
from $t=0$ to $t=2$ (shown above)?
q-21353.source_quote:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{({e}^{t})^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062586/assets/4aa2bca8faab077c47fb968882579233babe7d323ba3120088e8ea5599fbd570.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y=t$
from $t=0$ to $t=2$ (shown above)?
fields.source_quote:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{({e}^{t})^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ $P(x):{x}^{2}>x$

Given the predicate above, which of the following expresses the statement $∀x\in (1,\infty ),\,P(x)?$
q-216463.source_quote:
The universal quantifier "$∀$" means "for all." So, the statement 
$∀x\in (1,\infty ),\,P(x)$ 
reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $x\in (1,\infty ),$ ${x}^{2}>x.$

**Note:** This statement is true.

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=v(2-u),\,y=u{v}^{3}.
$$

The image of the side ${S}_{3}$ under the action of $T$ is given by

$$
x=x(t),\,y=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

Find the function $x(t).$
q-225023.source_quote:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{3}.$

For the side ${S}_{3},$ we have $1\ge u\ge 0$ and $v=1.$ Substituting $v=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(v(2-u),\,u{v}^{3}) \\  & =(1(2-u),\,u(1)^{3}) \\  & =(2-u,u).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{3}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=2-u,\,y=u,\,1\ge u\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x(t)=2-t,\,y(t)=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=\frac{v-1}{u+1},\,y=(u+v-1)^{2}+1.
$$

Which of the following is the image of the side ${S}_{4}$ under the action of $T?$
q-225228.source_quote:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{4}.$

For the side ${S}_{4},$ we have $u=0$ and $1\ge v\ge 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(\frac{v-1}{u+1},\,(u+v-1)^{2}+1) \\  & =(\frac{v-1}{0+1},\,(0+v-1)^{2}+1) \\  & =(v-1,\,(v-1)^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{4}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=v-1,\,y=(v-1)^{2}+1,\,1\ge v\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x=t-1,\,y=(t-1)^{2}+1,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

These are parametric equations of a parabolic arc. Notice that if we eliminate $t$ from the equations, we get

$$
y={x}^{2}+1
$$

which is an upward-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,1).$

Moreover, the endpoints of ${S}_{4}$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T:(0,1)\to (\frac{1-1}{0+1},(0+1-1)^{2}+1)=(0,1) \\  & T:(0,0)\to (\frac{0-1}{0+1},(0+0-1)^{2}+1)=(-1,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${S}_{4}$ is an arc of a upward-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,1)$ to $(-1,2).$

q-26223.source_problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.3x-0.1y=0.6 \\ 0.6x+0.8y=0.2\end{aligned}
$$
q-26223.source_quote:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.3x-0.1y=0.6 & |\,\times 10 \\ 0.6x+0.8y=0.2 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ 6x+8y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the second equation by $(-2),$ we will get a $-3x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $3x$ term in the first equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 &  \\ 6x+8y=2 & |\,÷(-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ -3x-4y=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3x}-y & =6 \\ -\cancel{3x}-4y & =-1 \\ (-y-4y) & =(6-1) \\ -5y & =5 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

fields.source_quote:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.3x-0.1y=0.6 & |\,\times 10 \\ 0.6x+0.8y=0.2 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ 6x+8y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the second equation by $(-2),$ we will get a $-3x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $3x$ term in the first equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 &  \\ 6x+8y=2 & |\,÷(-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ -3x-4y=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3x}-y & =6 \\ -\cancel{3x}-4y & =-1 \\ (-y-4y) & =(6-1) \\ -5y & =5 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=-1$ into the equation $3x-y=6$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y & =6 \\ 3x-(-1) & =6 \\ 3x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\frac{5}{3}$ and $y=-1.$

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
q-27482.source_quote:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.5.$ Therefore, $c=2.5.$

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
fields.source_quote:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.5.$ Therefore, $c=2.5.$

q-29163.source_problem:
Which of the following equations has no solutions for $0\le x<2\pi ?$

- $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=1$
- $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=2$
- $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}$
q-29163.source_quote:
Recall that the range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ for $0\le x<2\pi $ is given by

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation III has no solutions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996965/assets/a740aafbb9f74e2681506d3027f848fa92e7eea2bac3e08ccaf3fc7e0acf8fa1.png)

Which of the following systems of inequalities defines the shaded region shown in the graph above?
q-29384.source_quote:
Consider the line $y=x+2.$ Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict. Also, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y>x+2.
$$

    

Now consider the line $y=-x+1.$ Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y\ge -x+1.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$
{\begin{aligned}y>x+2 \\ y\ge -x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following systems of inequalities defines the shaded region shown in the graph above?
fields.source_quote:
Consider the line $y=x+2.$ Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict. Also, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y>x+2.
$$

    

Now consider the line $y=-x+1.$ Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y\ge -x+1.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$
{\begin{aligned}y>x+2 \\ y\ge -x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2939.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066033/assets/9283bcc77ac8e63c1ba00f9a81e659bcbcf41bc98b94a1a0617b02feab71cf0a.png)

Car $B$ is being driven due south toward Caltech at a speed of $60\,\text{km/h},$ while car $A$ is being driven due east away from Caltech. When car $B$ is $0.6\,\text{km}$ away from Caltech, car $A$ is $0.8\,\text{km}$ from Caltech. If the distance between the two vehicles is increasing at a rate of $20\,\text{km/h},$ what is the speed of car $A?$
q-2939.source_quote:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066033/assets/6e7ef0d4665710a31c1c601048498f20ad6b3099769c1d140320074805964ec7.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between Caltech and car $A$,

- $y$ is the distance between Caltech and car $B$,

- $z$ is the distance between the two cars.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $x,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=0.8\,\text{km}$ and $y=0.6\,\text{km}.$ We can find $z$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {0.8}^{2}+{0.6}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =1\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-60\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=20\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(0.8)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(0.6)(-60) & =2(1)(20) \\ 1.6\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =40+72 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{112}{1.6} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car $A$ is $70\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

q-2941.source_problem:
A rocket that is launched vertically is tracked by a radar station located on
the ground $3\,\text{km}$ from the launch site. What is the vertical speed of the rocket at the instant when its distance from the radar station is $5\,\text{km}$ and this distance is increasing at a rate of $1\,000\,\text{km/h}?$
q-2941.source_quote:
We start by drawing a diagram of the problem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069977/assets/7af033f137fd76e5e3003926a598e695f4e0852b11dc27dfa84d58040144972b.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between the radar station and the launch point,

- $y$ is the distance between the launch point and the rocket, and

- $z$ is the distance between the radar station and the rocket.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $y,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=3\,\text{km}$ and $z=5\,\text{km}.$ We can find $y$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {3}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={5}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =4\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=1\,000\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- the distance between the radar station and the launch point ($x$) remains the same, so $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(3)(0)+2(4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2(5)(1\,000) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{10\,000}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\,250\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertical speed of the rocket is $1\,250\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

q-30052.source_problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=9$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
q-30052.source_quote:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =9 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2})-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=9,$ and $p+q=7.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =9 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =2\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+3=5 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-3=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=5.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

fields.binding: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=9$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
fields.source_quote:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =9 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2})-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=9,$ and $p+q=7.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =9 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =2\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+3=5 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-3=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=5.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

q-30055.source_problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-2x+1=1$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,pq\,,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
q-30055.source_quote:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot x\cdot 1+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$ Thus, $pq=-1.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |x-1| & =1 \\ x-1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =1\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-1=0 \\ {x}_{2} & =1+1=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2.$

fields.binding: Original radio field 1 (selection): Completed square has p=-1,q=1; product -1 and roots 0,2 sum 2.
fields.source_quote:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot x\cdot 1+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$ Thus, $pq=-1.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |x-1| & =1 \\ x-1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =1\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-1=0 \\ {x}_{2} & =1+1=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2.$

q-31213.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14040224/assets/19e9763d62ca7818024bf49522a127a48dd04f76d1175c93e060a1043b6a5795.png)

The function $f(x)$ is continuous and twice-differentiable for all $x.$ The graph $y={f}^{″}(x)$ is shown above. At what value(s) of $x$ does $f(x)$ have a point of inflection?
q-31213.source_quote:
First, notice that since $f(x)$ is twice-differentiable, the tangent line to the graph exists for all real $x.$

Inflection points occur when a graph changes concavity. In order for the graph to change concavity, the value of the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x)$ must switch sign. So, we are looking for points where the graph of ${f}^{″}(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.

We can see that the graph $y={f}^{″}(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=0$ and $x=4.$ 

Therefore, $f(x)$ has points of inflection at $x=0$ and $x=4.$

q-31872.source_problem:
The inverse of the matrix $J$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
q-31872.source_quote:
We write down $J$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $J$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${J}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{J}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

fields.binding:
The inverse of the matrix $J$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
fields.source_quote:
We write down $J$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $J$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${J}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{J}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-31919.source_problem:
Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

*If $det(A)\ne 0,$ where $A$ is a $2\times 2$-matrix, then $A$ is $\text{__________}$ .*

- invertible
- **not ** invertible
- singular
q-31919.source_quote:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.  

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true ($det(A)\ne 0$), all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem, only option I gives a true statement:

- *If $det(A)\ne 0$ , then $A$ is invertible.* $\,✓$

q-31945.source_problem:
The inverse of the matrix $K$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
q-31945.source_quote:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $K$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${K}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

fields.binding:
The inverse of the matrix $K$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
fields.source_quote:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $K$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].

q-32247.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=4 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-32247.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 10 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now  

$$
{\begin{aligned} & {x}_{1}+10{x}_{3}=-8 \\  & {x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ and we have one free variable, ${x}_{3}.$ That means we need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ in terms of ${x}_{3}.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=-8-10{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}=6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}={x}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{3}$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8-10{x}_{3} \\ 6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}

fields.binding:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=4 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
fields.source_quote:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 10 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now  

$$
{\begin{aligned} & {x}_{1}+10{x}_{3}=-8 \\  & {x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ and we have one free variable, ${x}_{3}.$ That means we need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ in terms of ${x}_{3}.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=-8-10{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}=6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}={x}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{3}$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8-10{x}_{3} \\ 6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-32373.source_problem:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous at $t=0?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{t}^{2},\,7t+6,\,3-{t}^{3}⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨1,\,{t}^{2/3},\,t⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨{t}^{2},\,\sqrt[3]{t},\,2t+3⟩\end{aligned}
$$
q-32373.source_quote:
A vector-valued function is continuous at a point if and only if each of its components is continuous at that point. 

Let's consider the functions one-by-one. 

- The function $f(t)$ is continuous at $t=0$ because each of its components ${t}^{2}$, $7t+6$ and $3-{t}^{3}$are continuous at $t=0.$

- The function $g(t)$ is continuous at $t=0$ because each of its components $1$,  ${t}^{2/3}$ and $t$  are continuous at $t=0.$

- The function $h(t)$ is continuous at $t=0$ because each of its components ${t}^{2}$, $\sqrt[3]{t}$ and $2t+3$ are continuous at $t=0.$

Therefore, the answer is:

$\,$ All the functions are continuous at $t=0$

q-324453.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
q-324453.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
fields.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

q-324455.source_problem:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
q-324455.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we have $E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $x(t)=Eu(t)$, or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)={u}_{1}(t)-{u}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)={u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
fields.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we have $E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $x(t)=Eu(t)$, or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)={u}_{1}(t)-{u}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)={u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

q-32546.source_problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-32546.source_quote:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
fields.source_quote:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

q-32568.source_problem:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (0,\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨1+{t}^{2},\,-t+2,\,\sqrt{t}⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
q-32568.source_quote:
All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all $t\in (0,\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(0,\pi )$ if and only if each of 
 its component functions are differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (0,\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$  to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $(0,\pi )$, we have that   $g(t)$ is also differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,{sec}^{2}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second component of this vector, $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$, is undefined at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$,  we conclude that the function $h(t)$ is not differentiable on $(0,\pi ).$

Therefore, the answer is:

$\,$ $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ only

\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 6 & 9 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.source_quote:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 6 & 9 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 6 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -1 \\ \boxed{} & \boxed{} & \boxed{} \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.
$$

Consider the LU factorization of the matrix $A$ above. From left to right, what are the missing elements from the second row of the matrix $U?$
q-32772.source_quote:
The matrix $U$ in the LU decomposition is obtained from the original matrix $A$ by row-reducing using Gaussian elementation. In particular, to make $0$ at the position ${a}_{21}$ of the matrix $A,$ we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 6 & 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from left to right, the elements from the second row of $U$ are $0,-5,$ and $4.$

q-327976.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$*
q-327976.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$*
fields.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

q-327989.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
q-327989.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
fields.source_quote:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =c\,⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =⟨4ct,\,c{e}^{t},\,2c{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}=4ct \\ {e}^{t}=c{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}=2c{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} & =1\cdot 4t \\ {t}^{2} & =2t \\ {t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{2},\,{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{2},\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,2)$ and $(8,{e}^{2},2{e}^{2}).$

q-33203.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨-5,0,1⟩+t⟨-3,1,0⟩,\,Π:-3x+y-2z+27=0.
$$
q-33203.source_quote:
Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y-2z+27 & =0 \\ -3x+y-2z & =-27 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ ⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ -3(-5-3t)+1\cdot t-2\cdot 1 & =-27 \\ 15+9t+t-2 & =-27 \\ 10t & =-40 \\ t & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-4$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-5-3(-4),-4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(7,-4,1).$

fields.source_quote:
Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y-2z+27 & =0 \\ -3x+y-2z & =-27 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ ⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ -3(-5-3t)+1\cdot t-2\cdot 1 & =-27 \\ 15+9t+t-2 & =-27 \\ 10t & =-40 \\ t & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-4$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-5-3(-4),-4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(7,-4,1).$

q-332064.source_problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
q-332064.source_quote:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $9$ units to the left.

q-333360.source_problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-y(t)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?
q-333360.source_quote:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ 2x-y-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $-2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we obtain

$$
-3y-3=0\,⇒\,y=-1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-1)+1=0\,⇒\,x=0.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium point is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

fields.source_quote:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ 2x-y-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $-2$ and adding the result to the second equation, we obtain

$$
-3y-3=0\,⇒\,y=-1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-1)+1=0\,⇒\,x=0.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium point is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

q-333856.source_problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
q-333856.source_quote:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$
