q-79577.source_problem: Is the function $f(x,y,z)=2xyz-{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}z$ homogeneous? If so, what is its degree?
q-79577.source_quote:
A function $f(x,y,z)$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ if it satisfies the property

$$
f(tx,ty,tz)={t}^{n}f(x,y,z).
$$

So first, we compute $f(tx,ty,tz),$ and then we simplify by writing it as ${t}^{n}f(x,y)$ for some $n$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty,tz) & =2(tx)(ty)(tz)-(ty)^{3}+(ty)^{2}(tz) \\  & =2{t}^{3}xyz-{t}^{3}{y}^{3}+{t}^{3}{y}^{2}z \\  & ={t}^{3}(2xyz-{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}z) \\  & ={t}^{3}f(x,y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
f(tx,ty,tz)={t}^{3}f(x,y,z)
$$

and so the degree of the homogeneous function $f(x,y,z)$ is $3.$

q-79609.source_problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

- ${D}_{1}(y)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+y$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-xy$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=y\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$
q-79609.source_quote:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2} \\  & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{1}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =ax\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+bx\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-ax{y}_{1}-bx{y}_{2} \\  & =a[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x{y}_{1}]+b[x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})=a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.\,\times 
$$

q-79784.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79784.source_quote:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$

fields.binding:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
fields.source_quote:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{({x}^{4}+C)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79799.source_problem:
Given that ${y}_{1}(t)={e}^{-t}$ and ${y}_{2}(t)={e}^{4t}$ are solutions to the equation ${y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}-4y=0,$ which of the following must also be a solution to the equation?

- $y(t)={e}^{-t-1}$
- $y(t)=7{e}^{-t}-3{e}^{-4t}$
- $y(t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}}{4}$
q-79799.source_quote:
According to the superposition principle, if the functions ${y}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous, linear differential equation, and ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are constants, then $y(t)={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(t)$ is also a solution to the equation.

We're given that ${y}_{1}(t)={e}^{-t}$ and ${y}_{2}(t)={e}^{4t}.$ Therefore, the following function is also a solution:

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}
$$

Let's consider each option:

- The function $y(t)={e}^{-t-1}=\frac{{e}^{-t}}{e}$ is a solution of the given equation. Here, ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{e},{c}_{2}=0.$

- The function $y(t)=7{e}^{-t}-3{e}^{-4t}$ is **not** a solution of the given equation because ${e}^{-4t}$ is not a solution.

- The function $y(t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}}{4}$ is a solution of the given equation. Here, ${c}_{1}=0,{c}_{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

q-79847.source_problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79847.source_quote:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
fields.source_quote:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79950.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=yx+{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
q-79950.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =y(0)(0)+{e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)={y}^{′}x+y+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & ={y}^{′}(0)(0)+y(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{″}x+{y}^{′}+{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}={y}^{″}x+2{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & ={y}^{″}(0)(0)+2{y}^{′}(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+2(1)+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 3+⋯ \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=yx+{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
fields.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =y(0)(0)+{e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)={y}^{′}x+y+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & ={y}^{′}(0)(0)+y(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{″}x+{y}^{′}+{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}={y}^{″}x+2{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & ={y}^{″}(0)(0)+2{y}^{′}(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+2(1)+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 3+⋯ \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-79951.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-1.
$$
q-79951.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-1,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2(0)-y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=2-{y}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2-{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2-(1)(1)+(-1)(0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =-{y}^{″}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-(1)(1)+2(1)(0)+(-1)(1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot (-2)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-1.
$$
fields.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-1,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2(0)-y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=2-{y}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2-{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2-(1)(1)+(-1)(0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =-{y}^{″}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-(1)(1)+2(1)(0)+(-1)(1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot (-2)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-80373.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $H$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ b & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
q-80373.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-2,$ $b=7,$ and $c=1.$

fields.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-2,$ $b=7,$ and $c=1.$

Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-80389.source_quote:

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

q-80392.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $B$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}b & -3 \\ c & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
q-80392.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=5,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-1.$

fields.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=5,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-1.$

q-80493.source_problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
q-80493.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

fields.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

q-80496.source_problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
q-80496.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

fields.binding: Original radio field 1 (selection): Eigenvectors(1,2),(1,1) for1,-2; determinantP-1, BP=PD; other offered P invalid.
fields.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=y(1+x){e}^{x}+ax{y}^{3}+3{x}^{2},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=bx{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$
q-80766.source_quote:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y(1+x){e}^{x}+ax{y}^{3}+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2}+0 \\  & =(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(bx{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =b(1+x){e}^{x}-6x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+x){e}^{x}+3ax{y}^{2}=b(1+x){e}^{x}-6x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $(1+x){e}^{x}$ and $x{y}^{2},$ respectively, we see that $b=1$ and $a=-2.$

q-80825.source_problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
q-80825.source_quote:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

q-81202.source_quote:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3+4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{0+4-2x}{1-0} \\  & =4-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

q-81236.source_problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
T[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-81236.source_quote:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$

$$
T={{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$

q-81273.source_problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}\,\,v \\ u+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
q-81273.source_quote:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}\,\,v$ and $y(u,v)=u+{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={u}^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2uv & {u}^{2} \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2uv\cdot 2v-{u}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4u{v}^{2}-{u}^{2} \\  & =u(4{v}^{2}-u).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ u(4{v}^{2}-u) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equation $u(4{v}^{2}-u)=0$ defines a pair of intersecting curves in the $uv$-plane: the line $u=0$ and the parabola $u=4{v}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

fields.source_quote:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

q-81386.source_problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
q-81386.source_quote:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

fields.source_quote:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

q-8171.source_problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x}.$
q-8171.source_quote:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{4!}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $\sqrt{x}$ in the above expansion and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x} & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{4}}{4!}-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{6}}{6!}+⋯ \\  & =1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{24}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{720}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x}.$
fields.source_quote:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{4!}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $\sqrt{x}$ in the above expansion and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x} & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{4}}{4!}-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{6}}{6!}+⋯ \\  & =1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{24}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{720}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81985.source_problem:
Find the contrapositive of the following statement: 

$\,$ **If** it is not warm outside, **then** you need a jacket.
q-81985.source_quote:
In our conditional statement: 

- The antecedent is $A:$ It is not warm outside.

- The consequent is $B:$ You need a jacket.

The contrapositive of a conditional statement $A⇒B$ is given by 

$$
¬B⇒¬A.
$$

First, we write down the negations of $A$ and $B:$

- $¬A:$ It is warm outside.

- $¬B:$ You don't need a jacket.

Therefore, the contrapositive is the following: 

$\,$ If you don't need a jacket, then it is warm outside.

q-8306.source_problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
q-8306.source_quote:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

fields.binding: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
fields.source_quote:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

q-83217.source_problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
q-83217.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83429.source_problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
q-83429.source_quote:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To get an expansion for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we multiply this series by ${x}^{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={x}^{2}(x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{7}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
fields.source_quote:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To get an expansion for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we multiply this series by ${x}^{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={x}^{2}(x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{7}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83479.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14075482/assets/8ce943f8a77fe5756fdaf77185d8b59493ef0da95da3605f1f2416786f9ec394.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=xy-4$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 4},$ shown above.
q-83479.source_quote:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}y,\,x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0,\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,4⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,4) \\  & =(t)(4)-4 \\  & =4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,{t}^{2}) \\  & =(t)({t}^{2})-4 \\  & ={t}^{3}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3}-4)^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution $t=0$ inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one candidate point, $(0,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(2,4),\,(-2,4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(2,4)$ | $(-2,4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-4$ | $4$ | $-12$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-12$ at the point $(-2,4)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $4$ at the points $(2,4).$

fields.source_quote:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}y,\,x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0,\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,4⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,4) \\  & =(t)(4)-4 \\  & =4t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,4)$ and $(2,4)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,{t}^{2}) \\  & =(t)({t}^{2})-4 \\  & ={t}^{3}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3}-4)^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives one solution $t=0$ inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$
Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one candidate point, $(0,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain three candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(2,4),\,(-2,4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(2,4)$ | $(-2,4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-4$ | $4$ | $-12$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-12$ at the point $(-2,4)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $4$ at the points $(2,4).$

q-8360.source_problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=0\,.
$$
q-8360.source_quote:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{2(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

fields.binding:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=0\,.
$$
fields.source_quote:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{2(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

q-8369.source_problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
q-8369.source_quote:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

fields.binding: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
fields.source_quote:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

q-83710.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-83710.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

fields.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

q-83854.source_problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -1 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
q-83854.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -3 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

fields.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -2 \\ 6 & -3 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

q-83860.source_problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PD{P}^{-1}.$
q-83860.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

fields.source_quote:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we find the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives us the eigenverctor ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the $y$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ 9(0)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =9 \\ -{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {y}^{2} & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercepts are $(0,-6)$ and $(0,2).$

q-84592.source_problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 13\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ a & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & b\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
q-84592.source_quote:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=13,$ and $c=3.$

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 13\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

In conclusion, we get $a=2,$ $b=13,$ and $c=3.$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7},$ what is the value of $cot⁡\theta ?$
q-85640.source_quote:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/8c7889d63cf5894236bc5f5e24feb64ecf5a47acb2c07c807a4e65458a991232.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{45}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $cot⁡\theta =\frac{cos⁡\theta }{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
cot⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{2}{7})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})}=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}=-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}.
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{24}}{7} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7})}=-\frac{7}{2\sqrt{6}}=-\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}.
$$

q-86413.source_problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-4w+11=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-86413.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-4w+11) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0 \\ 4({w}^{2}+w) & =11 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}w+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =11 \\ 4[{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1 & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =11+1 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=12.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12 \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ \sqrt{{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3} \\ |w+\frac{1}{2}| & =\sqrt{3} \\ w+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ w & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-4w+11=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
fields.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-4w+11) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0 \\ 4({w}^{2}+w) & =11 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}w+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =11 \\ 4[{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1 & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =11+1 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=12.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12 \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ \sqrt{{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3} \\ |w+\frac{1}{2}| & =\sqrt{3} \\ w+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ w & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-86414.source_problem: The equation $-3{x}^{2}+36x-94=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
q-86414.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$
